chapters.title: Chapter 4: Valuing a Business on Its Own Cash Flows

lessons.title: Building a Simple DCF Step by Step

children.text: Everything so far now assembles into one model. A discounted cash flow has exactly five steps, and none of them involves mathematics harder than what you did in Lesson 4.1. The difficulty is not the arithmetic. It is being honest about the assumptions, because a DCF will politely return whatever number you ask it for.

body.text: A DCF is a forecast of cash, a judgment about risk, and an assumption about the distant future, arranged in a spreadsheet. Its output is exactly as good as those three inputs, and no more scientific than the weakest of them.

children.text: The Five Steps

body.caption: What a DCF does, in order

cells: Project revenue, margins, capital expenditure and working capital for five years
Turn operating profit into free cash flow for each year
Bring each year's cash flow back to today at the cost of capital
Value everything beyond the forecast period, and discount that too
Add the pieces to get enterprise value, then subtract net debt to reach equity value

children.text: The Company and the Assumptions

Konkan Ceramics, the Ratnagiri tile maker from Lesson 2.1, is being valued. It closed FY26 with revenue of ₹200 crore and a 20% EBITDA margin. Management and the valuer agree the following assumptions, and every one of them is a judgment that a buyer will challenge.

cells: Below the last three years, because the base is larger and a competitor has added capacity
No operating leverage benefit assumed, since power and clay costs move with volume
In line with the existing asset base and planned additions
Higher than depreciation, because the business is growing and needs capacity
Matches the current receivable and inventory pattern
Effective rate under the concessional corporate regime
Built in Lesson 2.3 from a 7.0% risk-free rate
Roughly long-run nominal growth for a mature building materials business

body.text: Capital expenditure of 8% of revenue against depreciation of 6% is not an accident. A growing company must spend more than it depreciates, or it is quietly shrinking its own capacity. Any model where capital expenditure sits below depreciation for five straight years while revenue grows 10% a year is describing a business that does not exist.

children.text: Steps 1 and 2: From Revenue to Free Cash Flow

body.caption: The same formula as Lesson 2.1, now applied to each forecast year

body.text: Look at the last row against the second. EBITDA grows from ₹44.0 crore to ₹64.4 crore, but free cash flow only creeps from ₹15.7 crore to ₹23.0 crore. Growth is eating most of the extra profit through capital expenditure and working capital. This is the single most useful thing a DCF shows you that a multiple never will.

body.title: Compute one year of free cash flow
body.prompt: In Year 1, EBIT after tax is ₹23.1 crore, depreciation is ₹13.2 crore, capital expenditure is ₹17.6 crore and working capital rises by ₹3.0 crore. What is free cash flow for the year, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹23.1 crore + ₹13.2 crore - ₹17.6 crore - ₹3.0 crore = ₹15.7 crore. Depreciation is added back because no cash left the business for it. Capital expenditure is subtracted because cash genuinely did leave.

children.text: Step 3: Discount Each Year

body.caption: Discounting the forecast at a 12.5% cost of capital (₹ crore)

body.title: Konkan Ceramics: forecast cash flow against its present value

children.text: The five forecast years together are worth about ₹66.7 crore in today's money. That is nowhere near the value of the company, because the business does not shut down at the end of year five.
Step 4: Value Everything After Year Five
The
terminal value
captures the rest of the company's life in one number. The standard approach assumes cash flows grow at a steady rate forever.

markDefs.definition: The value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period, calculated as a single figure at the end of the forecast and then discounted back to today.

body.caption: Calculated as at the end of year 5, then discounted back to today

children.text: For Konkan: ₹23.0 crore × 1.05 ÷ (12.5% - 5%) = about ₹321.8 crore, standing at the end of year 5. Discounted back at the year 5 factor of 0.555, that is about ₹178.6 crore today.

body.title: Calculate a terminal value
body.prompt: A company's final forecast year produces free cash flow of ₹30 crore. Long-run growth is assumed at 4% and the cost of capital is 13%. What is the terminal value as at the end of that year, in ₹ crore? Round to the nearest crore.
body.explanation: ₹30 crore × 1.04 ÷ (0.13 - 0.04) = ₹31.2 crore ÷ 0.09 = about ₹347 crore. Remember this figure sits at the end of the forecast period, so it still has to be discounted back to today before it can be added to anything.

children.text: Step 5: Add It Up and Cross the Bridge

body.label: Share of value sitting in the terminal value
body.context: Roughly three quarters of this company's entire valuation comes from a single formula about what happens after year five. That is normal for a DCF, and it is also the reason a DCF should never be presented as a precise number. Lesson 4.3 takes that formula apart.

body.title: Where Konkan Ceramics' enterprise value comes from

children.text: Never Present One Number
Change the cost of capital by a percentage point either way, and the long-run growth rate by a point either way, and you get nine equally defensible answers. Show the grid, not the midpoint.

body.text: The grid runs from about ₹199 crore to about ₹326 crore. Nobody changed a single thing about the tiles, the customers or the factory. Two assumptions moved by one percentage point each. Anyone who presents a DCF as "the value is ₹245.3 crore" without showing this table is either inexperienced or selling something.

body.title: Four ways to quietly inflate a DCF

children.text: Hockey stick forecasts.
Flat growth for two years, then a sudden acceleration in years 3 to 5 that the company has never achieved before.
Capital expenditure below depreciation.
Cash flow rises because the model stops maintaining the asset base.
Working capital held flat while revenue doubles.
Real businesses fund receivables and inventory as they grow.
A terminal growth rate near the cost of capital.
The denominator shrinks towards zero and the value explodes. Anything above long-run nominal GDP growth is a claim that the company eventually becomes the economy.
Each of these is defensible in isolation and devastating in combination. When reviewing any model, check these four first, before you look at anything else.

body.title: Which objection matters most?
body.question: A model values a ₹300 crore revenue company at ₹1,200 crore. Reviewing it, you find four issues. Which one would you raise first?
options: Revenue growth is 11% instead of the 10% the company achieved last year
The terminal growth rate is 9%, against a cost of capital of 12%
Depreciation is forecast as a fixed amount rather than a percentage of revenue
The tax rate used is 25% instead of 25.17%
body.explanation: The terminal growth rate sits in the denominator. At 12% minus 9% the divisor is 0.03, which roughly doubles the terminal value against a more sober 6% assumption, and terminal value is usually the majority of the answer. A 9% perpetual growth rate also implies the company outgrows the Indian economy forever. The other three issues are worth fixing but move the total by a rounding error in comparison.

body.title: The model on your desk
body.scenario: You are on the investment committee of a mid-sized group. A DCF supporting a ₹450 crore acquisition shows: revenue growth of 8% in years 1 and 2, then 22% in years 3 to 5; EBITDA margin rising from 14% to 21% over the period; capital expenditure at 3% of revenue against depreciation of 5%; working capital held constant in rupee terms; a WACC of 10.5% and terminal growth of 7%. Terminal value is 84% of the enterprise value. The target has grown 9% a year for the last five years at a stable 14% margin.
body.prompt: Write the four questions you would put to the deal team.
body.modelAnswer:
1. What changes in year 3 to take growth from 8% to 22%, and what changes to lift the margin by seven percentage points? The target has done 9% growth at a 14% margin for five years. If a new plant, a new channel or a price increase drives this, show it as a separate line with its own costs and its own capital expenditure, not as a smooth ramp.
2. Why is capital expenditure below depreciation while revenue nearly doubles? Either the model is understating the investment required, or the company is running down its asset base. Ask for maintenance and growth capital expenditure separately, with a schedule.
3. Why is working capital flat in rupee terms? If the target grows revenue by 22% a year, receivables and inventory grow too. Every rupee of that is cash the buyer funds, and it should be a deduction in each forecast year.
4. Justify a 10.5% WACC and 7% terminal growth together. A 3.5 percentage point gap in the denominator is what produces 84% of the value sitting in the terminal value. At 12.5% and 5%, the same forecast would produce a materially lower number. Show the sensitivity grid across both.

And one process point: I would ask for the model to be rerun on the target's own historical growth and margin, as a base case, with the improvement plan shown as a separate upside case that the seller is not paid for today.

body.title: The share nobody notices
body.textWithBlank: In a typical five year DCF, the majority of the value comes not from the forecast years but from the ___ value.
body.explanation: In this lesson's model about 73% of enterprise value sat beyond year five, which is why Lesson 4.3 is devoted entirely to that number.

body.title: Review any DCF in ten minutes
steps: Compare forecast growth and margins against the last five years of actuals
Check capital expenditure against depreciation, and ask for the split between maintenance and growth
Confirm working capital grows with revenue
Find the terminal growth rate and compare it against long-run nominal GDP growth
Compute what percentage of enterprise value sits in the terminal value
Check that the discount rate matches the cash flows: post-tax, rupee, and consistent with the capital structure
Ask for the sensitivity grid across the cost of capital and terminal growth
Cross-check the implied EV/EBITDA against what comparable companies trade at
Confirm the bridge from enterprise value to equity value uses current debt and cash

body.label: Damodaran: spreadsheets and valuation tools
body.description: Free DCF templates, from a simple two stage model to full versions. Build one from scratch once with your own company's numbers, and every valuation report you read afterwards becomes easier to interrogate.

cards.definition: The years modelled individually, usually five, sometimes ten for longer cycles.

cards.term: Free cash flow to the firm
cards.definition: EBIT after tax, plus depreciation, less capital expenditure and the working capital increase.
The value of everything beyond the forecast period, in one figure.
The perpetual growth assumed after the forecast. It must stay below long-run nominal economic growth.
A table of values across a range of discount rates and growth rates, shown instead of a single number.
The EV/EBITDA that the DCF answer works out to, used as a cross-check against comparable companies.
Spending needed just to sustain current capacity, as opposed to growth capital expenditure.

points: A DCF is five steps: forecast, convert to cash, discount, add a terminal value, and bridge to equity value.
Konkan Ceramics produced ₹66.7 crore of present value from five forecast years and ₹178.6 crore from the terminal value, for an enterprise value of about ₹245.3 crore.
After deducting ₹60 crore of net debt, equity value was about ₹185.3 crore, or roughly ₹92.7 a share on 2 crore shares.
About 73% of the value sat beyond year five, which is normal and is exactly why a DCF is a range rather than a number.
Moving the cost of capital and terminal growth by one point each swung enterprise value from about ₹199 crore to about ₹326 crore.
Growth consumes cash: EBITDA rose far faster than free cash flow because capital expenditure and working capital absorbed the difference.
The four classic inflation tricks are hockey stick forecasts, capex below depreciation, flat working capital, and a terminal growth rate close to the cost of capital.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Konkan Ceramics is fictional and every assumption in the model is illustrative. A DCF prepared for a transaction, a regulatory filing or financial reporting should be prepared or reviewed by a qualified valuer, with assumptions documented and supported.
